Chapter 1 — Did It Actually Work?

Causal Analysis in Public Health Management | BK Advisors

Matthew Luke Kuch | BK Advisors

2026-05-12

Meet Almaz

Almaz, 22, Tigray region, Ethiopia (a composite story drawn from DHS Ethiopia 2016 narratives — the details are real, the name is not)

It is 2015. Almaz is having her first baby.

She gives birth at home. Her mother is in the room. So is a young woman in a green uniform — a Health Extension Worker sent by the government.

The labour is long but the baby comes out crying. Both survive.

The question: Did the woman in the green uniform save Almaz’s baby? Or would the baby have been fine anyway?

And here is the puzzle

Between 2000 and 2016, maternal mortality in Ethiopia fell from 673 to 412 deaths per 100,000 live births (DHS Ethiopia 2000; 2016).

Over the same period, Ethiopia trained and deployed roughly 38,000 Health Extension Workers like the one in Almaz’s story (WHO 2013).

At first glance, this looks easy: more workers, fewer deaths. The program worked.

But here is the twist

In 2005, only 5 out of 100 Ethiopian women gave birth in a health facility.

By 2016, that number had risen — but only to 26 out of 100 (DHS Ethiopia 2005; 2016).

So most births in Ethiopia, including Almaz’s, were still happening at home during the years when mortality was falling fastest.

If most women were not going to clinics, then something other than “more clinic visits” was driving the drop. What?

What if I told you…

…there are three traps hiding inside that question?

  1. Two things happening together is not the same as one causing the other.

  2. A third thing you didn’t think of can be driving both.

  3. You have to draw the picture before you trust the numbers.

For the rest of this chapter, we are going to walk through these three traps using Almaz’s story.

Trap 1 — Two things together ≠ one caused the other

Every morning you see your neighbour walk out the door carrying an umbrella.

Every morning it rains.

The umbrella caused the rain.

Your neighbour checked the forecast. The forecast caused both — her umbrella and the rain landing on her head.

The lesson: Things that happen at the same time often share a cause. They do not always cause each other.

Trap 1 in Almaz’s story

The Health Extension Worker was in the room when Almaz’s baby cried.

But “in the room when it happened” is the same kind of evidence as “carrying an umbrella when it rained”.

The aha: We cannot tell from this one moment whether the HEW caused the safe birth, or whether she was simply present during a birth that would have gone fine anyway.

Trap 2 — A hidden third thing

Across many countries, ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together every summer.

Ice cream causes drowning.

Hot weather causes both — more people eat ice cream and more people swim.

The lesson: When two things move together, look for a hidden third thing — a confounder — that might be driving both.

Trap 2 in Almaz’s story

The same year the Health Extension Worker arrived in Almaz’s village, a new road also reached the village.

The road cut the trip to the nearest district hospital from four hours to ninety minutes.

So when something went wrong in a difficult birth, families could now reach a hospital in time. (Tigray Regional Health Bureau, 2014, public summary)

The aha: Was it the HEW? Was it the road? Was it both? You cannot tell which until you separate them — and “they arrived together” is exactly what makes it hard.

Trap 3 — Draw the picture first

When everything is tangled together — the HEW, the road, the school, the radio campaign, the new bus that brought the nurse — you need a way to see the tangle before you start counting things.

The tool we use is a directed acyclic graph. Don’t be intimidated by the name. It is just a picture made of boxes and arrows.

A box = a thing that can vary (the HEW being there or not; the road being open or not; the baby surviving or not).

An arrow = “this one influences that one”.

Trap 3 in Almaz’s story

Here is Almaz’s situation as a picture:


Government funding

⬇ ⬇

Health Extension Worker New road

⬇ ⬇

Almaz’s baby survives

The aha: Once you draw this, you can see why the simple question “did the HEW work?” cannot be answered without also asking about the road. They share a parent — the funding decision that paid for both.

Back to the puzzle

So what was actually going on?

The Lancet’s analysis of Ethiopia’s mortality decline points to three things at once — and probably others — moving in the same direction (Wang et al., Lancet Global Health, 2014):

  • Health Extension Workers in villages, doing antenatal visits and recognising danger signs
  • New roads and transport making it possible to actually reach a hospital when something went wrong
  • Girls staying in school longer, marrying later, having their first baby older

The hidden piece: “The program worked” is the wrong question. The right question is which parts worked, for whom, and how much — and you cannot answer that without first drawing the picture.

Why this matters

Almaz is one story. Ethiopia is one country. But the trap is everywhere.

Every time someone says “we did X and the outcome got better, so X worked” — about a vaccine campaign, a cash transfer, a school feeding programme, a new clinic — they are at risk of confusing all three traps.

The job of this course is to give you the tools to not make that mistake.

Try it yourself

You are the analyst

scenario

A neighbouring district to Almaz’s launches a free SMS reminder service for pregnant women in 2018. By 2020, antenatal visit rates in that district have risen by 12 percentage points.

The district health officer tells you the SMS service caused the rise. He wants more funding to expand it.

What is the first question you would ask him before recommending the funding?

Hint: think about what else might have changed in that district between 2018 and 2020.

In Chapter 2 we will turn this kind of question into a picture you can actually draw — and use that picture to decide what to ask next.

What you will do in R

On the companion page

When you go to the companion page for this chapter, you will write a few lines of R that draw Almaz’s diagram from earlier — the boxes for the HEW, the road, and the baby’s survival, with the funding box up top.

You will then ask R one specific question: if I add the road to my picture, does the apparent effect of the HEW change?

You do not need to install anything yet. The code on the companion page is there to read first, run later.

Looking ahead

In Chapter 2, we will learn how to draw these pictures properly — what the boxes can mean, what the arrows can mean, and what the rules are for connecting them.

By the end of Chapter 2, you will be able to draw a picture for any programme someone tells you about — even if you have never heard of it before.

Further reading

The data behind Almaz’s story

  • DHS Ethiopia, 2000 / 2005 / 2011 / 2016 — the four Demographic and Health Surveys this chapter draws from. All publicly available at dhsprogram.com.
  • WHO, 2013 — Success Factors for Women’s and Children’s Health: Ethiopia. The country case study on the Health Extension Worker programme.
  • Wang H. et al., 2014 — “Global, regional, and national levels of neonatal, infant, and under-5 mortality.” The Lancet, 384(9947). Open-access.

If you want to go deeper on the ideas

  • Ryall, M. D. & Bramson, A. L. (2014) — Inference and Intervention: Causal Models for Business Analysis. Routledge. The textbook this course is adapted from. Same tools, different setting — written for business decisions; we use them here for public health and MNH.
  • Pearl, J. & Mackenzie, D. (2018) — The Book of Why. The most readable introduction to causal inference ever written. Start with chapters 1 and 4.

The one thing to remember

Two things happening together is not the same as one causing the other.

Almaz’s baby lived. The HEW was in the room. So was a new road. So was a longer school year for girls. The whole job of causal analysis is figuring out which of those mattered — and how much.
